new_statements.translation: 1123. From the point of view of word accent, Pomeranian divides into two parts, of course not very sharply separated from each other: in one area the accent is free and mobile, in the other it is bound to the first syllable of the word. [...] 1124. As dialects with free and partly also mobile accent one must count the North Pomeranian and South Kashubian dialects, except the Parchowo dialect and the South-West Kashubian dialects; as dialects with immobile initial accent, the Parchowo dialect, the South-West Kashubian dialects, the Kashubian-Zaborian transitional dialects and the Zaborian ones. (Read from the page image; the scanned renders printed 'g' as 's'/'$'.)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Slovincian has an empty rule; this work supplies it: free, mobile (lexical/morphological) accent for the Slovincian dialects, as part of the North Pomeranian free-accent zone, against fixed initial accent in the southern zone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Slovincian belongs to the North Pomeranian group, where word accent is free (not tied to any syllable) and mobile within paradigms; fixed initial accent holds only in the southern group (Parchowo, SW Kashubian, transitional and Zaborian dialects), and Polish penultimate accent is spreading into the Zaborian border dialects (§ 1126, p. 605). § 1128 (p. 606): the mobile type with accent on the final suffix syllable in certain cases 'w większym zakresie jest tylko w gwarach słowińskich, główczyckiej, cecenowskiej i charbrowsko-łebskiej, jak również w jastarnickiej oraz w Kuzwelcie' (to a larger extent only in the Slovincian, Główczyce, Cecenowo and Charbrowo-Łeba dialects, and in Jastarnia and Kuzfeld).
new_statements.secondary_stress: § 1186, p. 642: in runs of three or more unstressed syllables the penultimate is regularly the strongest ('regularnie zgłoska przedostatnia jest najsilniejsza.. Ten przycisk poboczny na zgłosce przedostatniej jest właściwy wszystkim pomorskim gwarom'); a second, much stronger secondary accent occurs in compounds of two polysyllabic words, each member keeping its accent, one main and one secondary (§§ 1186-1187, pp. 642-643); p. 646: in polysyllabic pronoun + noun groups the pronoun's accent is weaker, 'akcentem pobocznym, co jednak na pewno stwierdziłem tylko dla słowińszczyzny' (confirmed with certainty only for Slovincian).
new_statements.exceptions: Vocative names and animal calls with final accent in southern dialects (§ 1125); Polish penultimate accent in Zaborian border dialects (§ 1126); many class-specific accent alternations for Slovincian and its neighbours throughout §§ 1127-1185 (nouns, adjectives, numerals, pronouns, verbs), with cross-references to Slovinzische Grammatik pp. 172 ff., 178, 187, 190.
new_statements.identity_note: The catalog item kash1274 is named Slovincian, but Glottolog kash1274 is Kashubian; Slovincian proper (Kluki/Smołdzino area, extinct) is slov1270. Lorentz 1927-37 treats the 'gwary słowińskie' as part of North Pomeranian and groups them with the Główczyce, Cecenowo and Charbrowo-Łeba dialects (the four dialects on German Pomerania) for the accent-quality and mobile-accent facts; Lorentz 1903 describes West and East Slovincian (Gardna and Smołdzino/Kluki). Hopkins 2001 lists Slovincian as dialect I of North Kashubian and gives no Slovincian-specific stress rule.

new_statements.quote: Most descriptions of Kashubian stress focus on the northern dialects and adopt a historical perspective, making determination of the default stress pattern difficult, but Kashubian can be characterized on the whole, as I have argued in Hopkins (1991, 1992), as having primary stress on the first syllable of the phonological or morphological word, with lexically stressed morphemes drawing stress away from this initial position. [...] There is little evidence for secondary stress: Lorentz (1925: 93) claims it falls on the initial syllable of compounds and the penultimate syllable of longer words with initial primary stress, but he does not mark it in his transcriptions of Kashubian speech

new_statements.relation_note: A whole-language generalization (default initial + lexical stress) that reframes Lorentz's northern 'free, mobile' accent as lexical stress overriding an initial default; it adds domain and secondary-stress detail but gives no Slovincian-specific placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Kashubian as a whole (Slovincian counted as dialect I of North Kashubian in his table, p. 26): default primary stress on the first syllable of the phonological/morphological word, overridden by lexically stressed morphemes; stress domain = clitic group in the south, prosodic word in the north; a trochaic foot is built over the lexically stressed syllable or else the first syllable; no rhythmic secondary stress, so no exhaustive footing. Slovincian itself is not described; Hopkins refers the reader to Lorentz 1903 and Stokhof 1973 (Kluki dialect, p. 12).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'There is little evidence for secondary stress' (p. 31); cites Lorentz 1925: 93 for secondary stress on the initial syllable of compounds and the penult of longer initially-stressed words, unmarked in Lorentz's transcriptions and only sporadic in the AJK and Topolinska.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically stressed morphemes; prepositions often (esp. southern dialects) included in the stress domain of the following word.

new_statements.quote: Der Wortakzent des Slovinzischen ist frei, d. h. er ist nicht wie der des Polnischen und Čechischen an eine bestimmte Silbe gebunden. Auch darin ist er unbeschränkt, dass er auf jede beliebige Silbe des Worts fallen kann und nicht etwa wie der des Griechischen an eine bestimmte Silbenzahl gebunden ist. In den einzelnen Paradigmen ist ein reger Akzentwechsel vorhanden. Es ist jedoch eine Tendenz zu bemerken, bei mehrsilbigen Stämmen, besonders in der Substantiv-, seltener in der Verbalflexion, den Akzent auf der ersten Silbe festzulegen.
new_statements.translation: The word accent of Slovincian is free, i.e. it is not, like that of Polish and Czech, bound to a particular syllable. It is also unrestricted in that it can fall on any syllable of the word whatsoever and is not, like that of Greek, bound to a particular number of syllables. Within the individual paradigms there is lively accent alternation. A tendency can however be noted, in polysyllabic stems, especially in noun and more rarely in verb inflection, to fix the accent on the first syllable. (scanned normalized: 'ist ist' and 'festzniegcn' in the djvu text read 'ist' and 'festzulegen'.)

new_statements.relation_note: The primary description of Slovincian proper (slov1270), cited by both Lorentz 1927-37 and Hopkins 2001; agrees with index 0 that Slovincian accent is free and mobile.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Free, mobile word accent, any syllable possible, with paradigmatic alternation and a tendency toward stem-initial fixing in polysyllabic stems; § 99 p. 171: end-stressed forms occur only with monosyllabic stems, and in polysyllabic stems the accent may not move beyond the last stem syllable. Two accent qualities (scharfer Ton on long-grade vowels, dehnender Ton on short-grade vowels), §§ 95-97.
new_statements.secondary_stress: § 108 p. 219: 'In einstämmigen nichtzusammengesetzten Wörtern ist nur eine Silbe durch den Akzent ausgezeichnet'; secondary accents only in compounds of two polysyllabic words (each keeps its accent, one main, one secondary), in va- prefixed nouns, in adjective compounds, and on the penult of superlatives of more than three syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Sporadic initial-accent forms that sound like speech errors (§ 98); the § 108 compound patterns.
new_statements.identity_note: The catalog item kash1274 is named Slovincian, but Glottolog kash1274 is Kashubian; Slovincian proper (Kluki/Smołdzino area, extinct) is slov1270. Lorentz 1927-37 treats the 'gwary słowińskie' as part of North Pomeranian and groups them with the Główczyce, Cecenowo and Charbrowo-Łeba dialects (the four dialects on German Pomerania) for the accent-quality and mobile-accent facts; Lorentz 1903 describes West and East Slovincian (Gardna and Smołdzino/Kluki). Hopkins 2001 lists Slovincian as dialect I of North Kashubian and gives no Slovincian-specific stress rule.

readall_conflicts: No source places Slovincian stress on a fixed syllable. Lorentz 1903 (§ 98) and Lorentz 1927-37 (§§ 1123-1124, 1128) both describe the Slovincian dialects as having free, mobile accent with paradigmatic alternation, against fixed initial accent in the southern Kashubian/Zaborian group. Hopkins 2001 (pp. 30-31) reframes Kashubian as a whole as default initial stress overridden by lexically stressed morphemes, admits that the northern (free-accent) dialects make the default hard to determine, and defers Slovincian itself to Lorentz 1903 and Stokhof 1973; this is a difference of analysis (lexical stress over an initial default vs. free accent) rather than a contradiction about Slovincian placement. Lorentz 1925 could not be opened; Hopkins reports its p. 93 claim on secondary stress only. Lorentz 1927-37 (p. 642) and Lorentz 1903 (§ 108) agree that non-compound words carry one accent and that secondary accents arise in compounds; Lorentz 1927-37 adds a rhythmic penultimate secondary prominence in runs of three or more unstressed syllables in all Pomeranian dialects, which Hopkins calls 'little evidence for secondary stress'.
